claims.text: Adding a nanometer-thick electroless-plated Ni interlayer to W particles increases the thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite retains mechanical durability relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite retains irradiation resistance relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated composite.
The proposed intervention is electroless plating of W particles with a 5–10 nm Ni layer before composite consolidation.
Sintering at approximately 1100–1200 °C in a controlled reducing atmosphere minimizes oxidation.
Maintaining the Ni layer at 5–10 nm limits excessive interdiffusion during processing.
The intervention produces a coherent, well-bonded Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer minimizes thermal boundary resistance between W and Cu.
Ni coating improves wetting between W and Cu.
Ni coating improves interfacial bonding between W and Cu.
Improved W–Cu interfacial contact reduces thermal boundary resistance.
Reduced thermal boundary resistance facilitates more efficient phonon and electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
A robust Ni interlayer helps sustain mechanical durability.
A robust Ni interlayer resists irradiation-induced degradation.
The Ni-modified composite should have mechanical strength matching or exceeding that of an uncoated W–Cu composite processed and operated under the same conditions.
The Ni-modified composite should have irradiation resistance matching or exceeding that of an uncoated W–Cu composite processed and operated under the same conditions.
Uncontrolled diffusion may form brittle Ni-containing intermetallic compounds that invalidate the expected benefits.
Formation of Ni–W or Ni–Cu compounds during sintering could impair mechanical integrity or irradiation resistance.
